questions.stem: Which list gives the states of chlorine, bromine and iodine at room temperature in the correct order?

options.text: Gas, liquid, solid
options.explanation: Chlorine is a pale yellow-green gas, bromine the only liquid halogen, and iodine a grey crystalline solid.

options.text: Solid, liquid, gas
options.explanation: That reverses the true order; states move from gas towards solid as you descend the group.

options.text: Gas, gas, liquid
options.explanation: Only fluorine and chlorine are gases at room temperature; iodine sits below bromine and is firmly a solid.

options.text: Liquid, gas, solid
options.explanation: Bromine is the middle element and the middle state; chlorine above it must be the gas.

questions.stem: Why do the melting and boiling points of the halogens rise down the group?

options.text: Larger atoms give stronger intermolecular forces, so more energy separates the molecules
options.explanation: Melting and boiling only have to overcome the forces between molecules, and those grow with molecular size down the group.

options.text: The covalent bonds inside the molecules get weaker
options.explanation: Melting and boiling do not break the covalent bonds at all; they only loosen the grip between whole molecules.
options.misconception: covalent bonds thought to break on melting

options.text: The molecules get heavier, and heavy things melt higher
options.explanation: Mass itself does not set melting point; the growth of intermolecular forces with molecular size does.

options.text: The metals inside the molecules pack closer together
options.explanation: The halogens are non-metals and their molecules contain no metals; the trend belongs to intermolecular forces.

questions.stem: A student records that iodine is a red-brown liquid at room temperature. Which halogen has actually been described?

options.text: Bromine, which is the dense red-brown volatile liquid
options.explanation: Red-brown liquid is bromine's description; iodine is the grey shimmery solid that sublimes to a purple vapour.

options.text: Iodine, as described
options.explanation: Iodine is a grey solid at room temperature; the red-brown liquid description belongs one place higher, to bromine.

options.text: Chlorine, which is dense and coloured
options.explanation: Chlorine is the pale yellow-green gas; no halogen above bromine is a liquid at room temperature.

options.text: Fluorine, the most reactive halogen
options.explanation: Fluorine is the yellow gas at the top of the group; reactivity says nothing about being a red-brown liquid.

questions.stem: What colour is the solution formed when iodine dissolves or is displaced into the aqueous layer?

options.text: Dark brown
options.explanation: Iodine in solution appears dark brown, which is how its displacement is spotted in the halogen tests.

options.text: Orange
options.explanation: Orange in solution is bromine's colour; iodine darkens the solution to brown.
options.misconception: bromine and iodine solution colours swapped

options.text: Pale green
options.explanation: Pale green belongs to chlorine in solution, the least coloured of the three halogens tested.

options.text: Colourless, because iodine is a grey solid
options.explanation: Once dissolved or displaced into solution, iodine clearly colours the liquid dark brown.
options.misconception: solid appearance carried over into solution

questions.stem: Why do all halogens have similar chemical reactions?

options.text: Each halogen atom has seven electrons in its outermost shell
options.explanation: Reactivity is governed by outer-shell electrons, so the shared seven-electron outer shell gives the group one common reaction pattern.

options.text: They are all diatomic molecules
options.explanation: Diatomic bonding describes how the atoms pair up; the similar chemistry comes from the seven outer electrons.
options.misconception: molecular form mistaken for the cause

options.text: They are all gases at room temperature
options.explanation: Bromine is a liquid and iodine a solid; physical state has no bearing on the shared chemistry.

options.text: They all have the same number of protons
options.explanation: Each halogen has a different proton count; identical protons would make them one element rather than a group.
options.misconception: element identity confused with its reactions

questions.stem: Aluminium forms Al3+ ions. Which formula would aluminium bromide take?

options.text: AlBr3
options.explanation: Each bromide carries a single 1- charge, so three bromide ions are needed to cancel the 3+ charge on aluminium.

options.text: AlBr
options.explanation: One bromide leaves a net 2+ charge; the halide's single negative charge forces a three-to-one ratio here.

options.text: Al3Br
options.explanation: The counts sit on the wrong ions; the three belongs to the bromide count, not to aluminium.

options.text: Al2Br3
options.explanation: These counts leave the charges unbalanced: six positive against three negative, so the salt cannot be neutral.

questions.stem: Iron reacts slowly with which pair of halogens, compared with the vigorous reaction with chlorine?

options.text: Bromine and iodine
options.explanation: Reactivity falls down the group, so bromine and especially iodine react more slowly with iron than chlorine does.

options.text: Fluorine and chlorine
options.explanation: Fluorine and chlorine are the top two for reactivity; iron reacts with them at least as vigorously as with chlorine alone.

options.text: Neither, because iron is unreactive with all halogens
options.explanation: Iron does form halide salts; the point is that the reaction rate slackens with the less reactive halogens.

options.text: It depends only on the temperature of the iron
options.explanation: Temperature matters, but the group trend fixes which halogen reacts faster at the same conditions.
options.misconception: conditions thought to override the trend

questions.stem: Which halogen reacts with hydrogen in the absence of light and at low temperature?

options.text: Fluorine
options.explanation: Fluorine, the most reactive halogen, combines with hydrogen explosively even in the cold and the dark.

options.text: Chlorine
options.explanation: Chlorine reacts with hydrogen but needs light or a high temperature to do so.

options.text: Iodine
options.explanation: Iodine reacts with hydrogen least vigorously of the three, and only slowly even with heating.

options.text: All halogens react identically with hydrogen
options.explanation: The conditions differ sharply down the group, which is precisely the evidence for the falling reactivity trend.
options.misconception: uniform vigour assumed across the group

questions.stem: Astatine sits below iodine in Group 7. Which prediction is consistent with the trend?

options.text: Astatine will be a darker solid than iodine and will react even more slowly with metals
options.explanation: Colours darken and reactivity falls on descending the group, so astatine should out-do iodine on both counts.

options.text: Astatine will be a pale gas lighter in colour than chlorine
options.explanation: Both statements contradict the trend: states move towards solid, and colours darken, on going down the group.

options.text: Astatine will displace iodine from potassium iodide solution
options.explanation: Displacement only runs from the more reactive halogen downwards, and astatine sits below iodine.

options.text: Astatine will not form halide salts at all
options.explanation: The group pattern promises salts with metals; only the vigour should weaken, not the pattern itself.

questions.stem: Why is the rate of reaction slower for halogens further down the group when they attack metals such as iron?

options.text: The increased distance from the nucleus to the outer shell weakens the pull on the electron being gained
options.explanation: Larger atoms hold their incoming electron less strongly, so the halogen attacks the metal less vigorously.

options.text: Lower halogens are lighter and drift away from the metal
options.explanation: Halogens get heavier, not lighter, down the group; the slowing comes from weakened electron attraction.

options.text: Their salts block the metal surface after the first few seconds
options.explanation: Slower reaction down the group is intrinsic to the halogen's electron gain, not a coating effect of its products.
options.misconception: product layer invented as the cause

options.text: The metal's valency changes with each halogen
options.explanation: The metal keeps its own valency; it is the halogen's reactivity that varies down the group.
options.misconception: metal property blamed for halogen trend

questions.stem: What is observed when chlorine solution is added to colourless potassium bromide solution?

options.text: The solution turns orange as bromine is displaced
options.explanation: Chlorine is above bromine in the group, so it displaces bromide ions and the freed bromine colours the solution orange.

options.text: The solution turns brown as iodine is displaced
options.explanation: There is no iodine in potassium bromide; the displaced halogen here is bromine, and brown is iodine's colour.

options.text: No reaction, because bromine is more reactive than chlorine
options.explanation: Chlorine sits above bromine in Group 7, so it is the more reactive of the pair and displacement does occur.

options.text: The solution becomes colourless as the bromide is destroyed
options.explanation: The bromide ions are converted into bromine molecules, which are orange in solution, not colourless.

questions.stem: Which displacement does bromine perform in aqueous solution?

options.text: Bromine displaces iodine from potassium iodide solution
options.explanation: Bromine is above iodine in Group 7, so it takes iodine's place in the salt and iodine colours the solution brown.

options.text: Bromine displaces chlorine from potassium chloride solution
options.explanation: Chlorine is above bromine, so potassium chloride shows no reaction with bromine solution.

options.text: Bromine displaces both chloride and iodide ions
options.explanation: Bromine can only displace halogens below itself; chloride sits above it and resists displacement.

options.text: Bromine displaces nothing at all in solution
options.explanation: Bromine does displace iodide; only iodine, at the bottom of the trio, displaces nothing.

questions.stem: Which word equation describes the reaction of chlorine with potassium iodide solution?

options.text: chlorine + potassium iodide → potassium chloride + iodine
options.explanation: The chlorine takes the iodide's place, so the metal pairs with chlorine and the iodine is set free.

options.text: chlorine + potassium iodide → potassium iodine + chloride
options.explanation: The metal keeps its partner swapped, not its name: the salt formed is potassium chloride, and iodine is released.

options.text: chlorine + potassium iodide → no reaction
options.explanation: Chlorine outranks iodine, so this pairing reacts readily with a visible brown colour.

options.text: potassium + iodine → potassium iodide
options.explanation: That is a synthesis reaction of the elements; the question concerns chlorine displacing iodine from the finished salt.

questions.stem: Why do displacement reactions give evidence for the reactivity trend of Group 7?

options.text: Each successful displacement shows the added halogen is the more reactive of the pair
options.explanation: Displacement only runs downhill, so the outcomes of the three pairings directly reveal the reactivity order.

options.text: The colours of the halogens alone prove the trend
options.explanation: Colours identify which halogen formed; the evidence is the pattern of which displacements succeed and which fail.
options.misconception: colour recall mistaken for the evidence

options.text: The salts change state during every displacement
options.explanation: Everything stays in aqueous solution; what changes is which halogen is present as molecules.
options.misconception: state change invented as the evidence

options.text: The reactions only work with potassium salts
options.explanation: Potassium salts are the usual choice, but the evidence comes from the halogen ordering, not the metal chosen.

questions.stem: A student mixes iodine solution with potassium chloride solution. What happens, and why?

options.text: No reaction, because iodine is less reactive than chlorine and cannot displace it
options.explanation: Displacement runs only from the more reactive halogen downwards, and iodine sits below chlorine in the group.

options.text: Chlorine is displaced and the solution turns pale green
options.explanation: That would require iodine to outrank chlorine, which is the reverse of the true order.

options.text: The solution turns brown as iodine dissolves further
options.explanation: Without a reaction there is no fresh iodine to release; a possible faint tint from the added solution is not a displacement.

options.text: Potassium metal is displaced and floats on the surface
options.explanation: Halogen displacement swaps the halogen partner, never releases the metal from its salt.
